title.en: Section 1 - A conversation about booking a holiday
title.zh: 第一部分 - 关于预订假期的对话

sections.passage: A conversation between a customer, Sarah, and a travel agent, Tom, about booking a holiday. Sarah calls the travel agency to arrange a trip to Bali, Indonesia. She wants to travel in mid-August for two weeks. Tom checks availability and finds that flights are available departing on August 14th and returning on August 28th. The flight departs from London Heathrow at 10:30 AM with a brief stopover in Singapore before arriving in Bali at 9:15 AM the following morning. Sarah asks about accommodation options. Tom recommends three hotels: the Beachfront Resort at 120 pounds per night with a sea view, the Garden Villas at 85 pounds per night with a pool view, and the City Centre Hotel at 65 pounds per night. Sarah prefers the Garden Villas because it offers a good balance of comfort and price. Tom mentions that the package includes breakfast but lunch and dinner are not included. However, the hotel has two restaurants on-site. Sarah also asks about airport transfers, and Tom says they are included in the package price. The total cost for the trip including flights and accommodation comes to 2,380 pounds for two people. Sarah asks about travel insurance, which is an additional 75 pounds per person. She decides to book the trip and provides her credit card details for a deposit of 500 pounds. Tom confirms the booking and says he will send a confirmation email with all the details within 24 hours.

title.en: Section 2 - A talk about a new leisure centre
title.zh: 第二部分 - 关于新休闲中心的介绍

sections.passage: A radio broadcast about the opening of a new community leisure centre in the town of Millfield. The presenter, Helen Grant, interviews the centre manager, James Wilson, about the facilities and services available. The leisure centre, which cost 12 million pounds to build, officially opens next Monday. It features a 50-metre Olympic-standard swimming pool, a fully equipped gym with over 200 pieces of exercise equipment, four indoor tennis courts, and a sports hall for basketball and badminton. There is also a dedicated children's area with a soft play zone and climbing walls. The centre will be open from 6 AM to 10 PM on weekdays and from 8 AM to 8 PM on weekends. Annual membership costs 450 pounds for adults, 300 pounds for students and senior citizens, and 200 pounds for children under 16. There is also a family membership option at 900 pounds which covers two adults and up to three children. Non-members can use the facilities on a pay-as-you-go basis, with swimming sessions costing 8 pounds and gym sessions costing 10 pounds. The centre also offers a range of fitness classes including yoga, pilates, spinning, and aqua aerobics, which are included in the membership fee. James mentions that they have hired 30 qualified staff members, including personal trainers who can create individual fitness programmes. A special opening promotion offers a 20 percent discount on annual memberships purchased before the end of the month.

title.en: Section 3 - A discussion about a university assignment
title.zh: 第三部分 - 关于大学作业的讨论

sections.passage: A conversation between two university students, Emma and Jack, discussing their upcoming group assignment for a Marine Biology course. They need to prepare a presentation on the impact of plastic pollution on marine ecosystems. Emma has been researching the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, which is the largest accumulation of ocean plastic in the world, located between Hawaii and California. She found that it covers an area of approximately 1.6 million square kilometres, which is roughly three times the size of France. Jack has been looking at the effects of microplastics on marine food chains. He discovered that microplastics, which are pieces smaller than 5 millimetres, are consumed by small fish and plankton, and then accumulate as they move up the food chain through a process called bioaccumulation. They decide to divide the presentation into three main sections: the sources and scale of ocean plastic pollution, the biological effects on marine organisms, and potential solutions. For the solutions section, Emma wants to focus on the Ocean Cleanup project, which uses floating barriers to collect plastic from the ocean surface. Jack suggests including information about biodegradable plastic alternatives made from seaweed, which are being developed by several research laboratories. They agree to meet in the library on Thursday afternoon to compile their research and create the presentation slides. Their professor, Dr. Mitchell, has asked them to keep the presentation to 15 minutes with 5 minutes for questions. Emma also mentions that they should include recent statistical data from the United Nations Environment Programme report published last year.

title.en: Section 4 - A lecture on urban green spaces
title.zh: 第四部分 - 关于城市绿地的讲座

sections.passage: A university lecture by Professor Anna Roberts on the importance of urban green spaces for sustainable city development. The professor begins by defining urban green spaces as any vegetated areas within cities, including parks, gardens, street trees, green roofs, and community gardens. She explains that these spaces provide multiple benefits known as ecosystem services. The first major benefit is temperature regulation. Cities with extensive green spaces can be up to 5 degrees Celsius cooler than those without, because vegetation absorbs sunlight and provides shade. This is particularly important as global temperatures continue to rise. The second benefit is air quality improvement. A single mature tree can absorb approximately 22 kilograms of carbon dioxide per year and produce enough oxygen for two people. Professor Roberts then discusses the psychological benefits of green spaces. Research conducted at the University of Exeter found that people who spend at least 120 minutes per week in natural environments report significantly higher levels of health and wellbeing. She also mentions a study from the Netherlands which showed that residents living within 300 metres of a green space had lower rates of anxiety and depression. The lecture moves on to discuss challenges facing urban green spaces, including land pressure from developers, maintenance costs, and the effects of climate change on urban vegetation. Professor Roberts presents the example of Singapore, which has successfully integrated green spaces into its urban planning through its City in a Garden initiative, achieving a green cover of approximately 47 percent despite being one of the most densely populated countries in the world. She concludes by arguing that cities must prioritise green infrastructure in their long-term planning strategies.

title.zh: 文章1 - 巧克力的历史

sections.passage: Chocolate is one of the most popular foods in the world, but its history stretches back thousands of years to the ancient civilizations of Central and South America. The cacao tree, from which chocolate is derived, is native to the tropical regions of the Americas, and its scientific name, Theobroma cacao, literally means 'food of the gods'. The earliest known use of cacao dates back to approximately 1900 BC, based on chemical analysis of ancient pottery vessels found in what is now Honduras. The Olmec civilization, which flourished in southern Mexico from around 1500 BC, is believed to have been the first to cultivate cacao plants and process the beans into a bitter drink. This practice was later adopted by the Maya and Aztec civilizations, who considered cacao to be a sacred gift from the gods. The Maya prepared a frothy beverage by mixing ground cacao beans with water, chilli peppers, and cornmeal, while the Aztecs added vanilla and other spices to create a drink called xocolatl, which means 'bitter water' in the Nahuatl language. Cacao beans were so valuable that the Aztecs used them as a form of currency. When the Spanish conquistador Hernan Cortes arrived in Mexico in 1519, he observed the Aztec emperor Montezuma drinking xocolatl and brought cacao beans back to Spain. The Spanish modified the recipe by adding sugar and honey to counteract the bitterness, creating a sweetened version that became popular among the European aristocracy. Over the next two centuries, chocolate drinking spread throughout Europe, and by the 17th century, chocolate houses had become fashionable social gathering places in London, similar to coffee houses. The invention of the chocolate bar in 1847 by Joseph Fry, a British chocolatier, marked a turning point in chocolate history. Fry discovered that by mixing cocoa powder, sugar, and cocoa butter, he could create a mouldable paste that could be shaped into solid bars. This innovation led to the establishment of numerous chocolate companies, including Cadbury, Lindt, and Nestle, which continue to dominate the global chocolate market today.

title.en: Passage 2 - The Rise of Electric Vehicles
title.zh: 文章2 - 电动汽车的崛起

sections.passage: The global automotive industry is undergoing its most significant transformation since the introduction of the assembly line over a century ago. Electric vehicles, once dismissed as impractical novelties, are rapidly becoming the dominant force in personal transportation. In 2022, global electric vehicle sales exceeded 10 million units, representing approximately 14 percent of all new car sales worldwide. This figure is expected to rise dramatically over the coming decade as governments implement increasingly strict emissions regulations and battery technology continues to improve. The transition to electric vehicles is being driven by several interconnected factors. Environmental concerns are perhaps the most significant. The transportation sector accounts for approximately 25 percent of global carbon dioxide emissions, and passenger vehicles are responsible for roughly half of that figure. By switching from internal combustion engines to electric motors powered by renewable energy sources, it is possible to reduce the carbon footprint of personal transportation by up to 70 percent. The falling cost of lithium-ion batteries has also been a crucial factor. In 2010, the average cost of a lithium-ion battery pack was approximately 1,200 dollars per kilowatt-hour. By 2022, this figure had fallen to around 130 dollars per kilowatt-hour, making electric vehicles increasingly competitive with conventional petrol and diesel cars in terms of purchase price. Industry analysts predict that battery costs will continue to decline, reaching approximately 80 dollars per kilowatt-hour by 2026, which would make electric vehicles cheaper to manufacture than their fossil fuel equivalents. However, the transition to electric vehicles faces several challenges. The most commonly cited concern is range anxiety, which refers to the fear that a vehicle's battery will run out of power before reaching a destination or charging station. While early electric vehicles had ranges of less than 100 miles, modern models can typically travel between 200 and 350 miles on a single charge, and some premium models exceed 400 miles. Charging infrastructure remains a significant barrier to adoption, particularly in rural areas. Governments and private companies are investing heavily in expanding charging networks, with the European Union aiming to install one million public charging points by 2025. The environmental impact of battery production and disposal also raises concerns, as the mining of lithium, cobalt, and nickel required for battery manufacturing can cause significant ecological damage.

sections.passage: Human beings like to think of themselves as rational creatures who carefully weigh up the pros and cons before making important decisions. However, decades of research in cognitive psychology and behavioural economics have revealed that our decision-making processes are far more complex and flawed than we might assume. One of the most influential contributions to this field was made by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky in the 1970s, when they developed Prospect Theory, which describes how people make choices involving risk and uncertainty. Their research demonstrated that people tend to weigh losses more heavily than equivalent gains, a phenomenon known as loss aversion. For example, most people would find losing 100 pounds more painful than the pleasure they would gain from winning the same amount. This asymmetry in how we perceive gains and losses has profound implications for everything from personal finance to public policy. Another important concept in decision-making research is the anchoring effect. This occurs when people rely too heavily on the first piece of information they encounter when making decisions. In a famous experiment, Kahneman and Tversky asked participants to spin a wheel that would land on either 10 or 65, and then estimate the percentage of African countries that are members of the United Nations. Those who spun 10 gave significantly lower estimates than those who spun 65, even though the number on the wheel was entirely random and had no logical connection to the question. The availability heuristic is another cognitive bias that affects our judgement. This refers to the tendency to overestimate the likelihood of events that are easily recalled, typically because they are recent, dramatic, or emotionally charged. For instance, after hearing about a plane crash, many people become temporarily more fearful of flying, even though statistically, air travel remains far safer than driving. Confirmation bias, the tendency to seek out and favour information that confirms our existing beliefs while ignoring contradictory evidence, is perhaps the most pervasive cognitive bias. Research has shown that this bias affects not only everyday decisions but also professional judgements in fields such as medicine, law, and scientific research. Understanding these cognitive biases is essential for improving decision-making quality. Many organisations now incorporate debiasing techniques into their processes, such as using structured decision frameworks, encouraging devil's advocate perspectives, and implementing blind evaluation procedures.
